subChunks.title: Feature Branches, Pull Requests & Commit Discipline
subChunks.hookHtml: In a professional team, nobody commits directly to main. Work flows through branches, pull requests, and code review. Understanding these workflows is not just a tool skill — it shapes how your team builds software safely.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Feature Branch Workflow

  1. Create a branch from main: git checkout -b feature/spell-search
  2. Commit work incrementally as you build
  3. Push to remote: git push -u origin feature/spell-search
  4. Open a Pull Request (PR) for review
  5. Address review comments, push more commits
  6. Merge to main when approved and CI passes
  7. Delete the branch

Commit Message Discipline — Conventional Commits

A widely adopted standard for commit messages:

<type>(<scope>): <short description>

[optional body]
[optional footer]

Examples:
feat(spells): add binary search to spell registry
fix(auth): prevent token expiry on concurrent requests
refactor(mage): extract validation into MageValidator
docs(api): update spell endpoint documentation
test(encoding): add edge-case tests for null feynmanPrompt
chore(deps): upgrade Jackson to 2.16.1

Types: feat (new feature), fix (bug fix), refactor, test, docs, chore (maintenance), perf (performance), ci.

Rebase vs Merge

  • Merge: creates a merge commit preserving the full branch history. Keeps context; main history has multiple lines.
  • Rebase: replays your commits on top of the target branch. Produces a linear history; each commit appears as if written directly after the latest main commit.
# Merge
git checkout main
git merge feature/spell-search

# Rebase (on your feature branch)
git rebase main
# Resolves conflicts per-commit; then:
git checkout main
git merge --ff-only feature/spell-search

Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch — rewriting shared history causes divergence for all other developers.

Small, Atomic Commits

Each commit should represent one logical change. If the commit message needs the word 'and', it probably contains two commits. Atomic commits make git bisect, code review, and revert far easier.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's collaborative spellbook has one catastrophic rule: never write directly on the master page. Every enchanter works on a personal draft — a branch — until their changes are reviewed and approved.

storyBeats.speaker: Arcane SCM Lead Finn
storyBeats.text: Feature branches are the fundamental unit of collaborative development. One task, one branch, one pull request. Never commit directly to main. The pull request is not just a review mechanism — it is the record of why a change was made, who approved it, and what the CI said.

storyBeats.speaker: Arcane SCM Lead Finn
storyBeats.text: Conventional commits are a naming standard for commit messages. Type first: feat, fix, refactor, test, docs, chore. Then scope in parentheses. Then a short description. The result is a machine-readable history that can generate changelogs automatically and make searching history practical.

storyBeats.speaker: Good vs bad commit messages
storyBeats.text:
# BAD
git commit -m "stuff"
git commit -m "wip"
git commit -m "fixed it"
git commit -m "changes"

# GOOD (conventional commits)
git commit -m "feat(spells): add pagination to spell list endpoint"
git commit -m "fix(auth): handle expired JWT in refresh endpoint"
git commit -m "test(mage): cover null name in registration flow"

storyBeats.speaker: Arcane SCM Lead Finn
storyBeats.text: Rebase vs merge is a team preference, but understand what each does. Merge preserves the full branching story. Rebase creates a clean linear history as if you'd written everything on top of the latest main — easier to read, but rewrites commit hashes. Never rebase shared branches — only private ones.

learningObjectives: Execute the full feature branch workflow: branch, commit, push, PR, merge, delete
Write conventional commit messages with the correct type, scope, and description
Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase and when to use each
Define an atomic commit and explain why small commits improve code review and debugging
commonMistakes: Committing directly to main instead of a feature branch
Writing vague commit messages ('fix', 'wip', 'stuff') — future-you will hate present-you for this
Rebasing a branch that has been pushed and shared with other developers
Making large commits with unrelated changes — makes code review painful and revert risky
assessmentCriteria: Can describe the full feature branch workflow including when to open a PR and what happens after merge
Can write five conventional commit messages for hypothetical changes (one feat, one fix, one refactor, one test, one chore)
Can explain what git rebase does to commit history and when it is unsafe
Can explain what 'atomic commit' means and give an example of a commit that should be split into two
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the feature branch workflow to a developer who has only ever committed directly to main. Why are branches important? What does a pull request add? What is the difference between merge and rebase?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Answer the following scenarios in writing:

  1. You are about to add a new REST endpoint for creating mages. Write the git branch name and three commit messages (using conventional commits) you might make during development.
  2. Your feature branch has diverged from main while you were working. Should you rebase or merge? State your reasoning and write the commands.
  3. A colleague suggests squashing all 12 commits on a feature branch before merging to keep main history clean. What are the trade-offs?
  4. You accidentally commit a password to main. What are the two most important immediate actions?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Branch: git checkout -b feature/create-mage-endpoint
   Commits:
   feat(mage): add POST /api/mages endpoint with validation
   test(mage): cover missing name and invalid tier in creation
   docs(api): document mage creation request/response shape

2. Rebase preferred here (private feature branch, not shared):
   git checkout feature/my-branch
   git rebase main
   # Resolve any conflicts per-commit
   # Then merge:
   git checkout main
   git merge --ff-only feature/my-branch
   Reason: Produces linear history; the feature appears as if written after the latest main changes.

3. Trade-offs of squashing:
   Pros: main history is clean — one meaningful commit per feature, easy to read
   Cons: fine-grained history (individual fixup commits) is lost — harder to bisect if the problem was introduced mid-feature
   Compromise: squash trivial fixup/wip commits but keep meaningful logical commits separate.

4. Immediate actions:
   1. Rotate the credential immediately — assume it has been seen
   2. Use git filter-branch or git-filter-repo to rewrite history and remove the secret, then force-push
   (Never just 'delete the file in a new commit' — the secret is still in git history)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
A colleague sends you a PR with the following commit history. Review it and suggest improvements:

abc1234 stuff
def5678 more changes
789abcd fixed the bug from yesterday
def0123 wip
456789a final version!!!

For each commit: identify what's wrong with the message and propose a conventional commit replacement. Then suggest whether these should be squashed, kept separate, or reorganised, and why.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Reviewing the commits:
1. 'stuff' — completely uninformative. No way to know what changed or why.
   Replacement: feat(spells): add mana cost field to spell creation form

2. 'more changes' — same problem. One word, no context.
   Replacement: refactor(spells): extract validation into SpellValidator class

3. 'fixed the bug from yesterday' — references external context ('yesterday') that won't make sense in 6 months. Which bug?
   Replacement: fix(mage): prevent NPE when mage has no assigned school

4. 'wip' — never commit WIP to a PR. Either squash it into the related commit or finish the work first.
   Should be squashed into the commit it relates to.

5. 'final version!!!' — enthusiasm doesn't belong in commit messages, and 'final' is never true.
   Replacement: chore(cleanup): remove debug log statements and TODO comments

Recommendation: squash commits 1, 2, 4, 5 if they all relate to one feature; keep commit 3 separate as it's a distinct bug fix. Rewrite all messages using conventional commits.

questions.prompt: What is the correct conventional commit type for adding a new API endpoint?
questions.explanation: feat is for new features — functionality that did not previously exist. fix is for bug corrections. chore is for maintenance tasks (dependency updates, build config). docs is for documentation changes.

questions.prompt: It is safe to rebase a feature branch after it has been pushed to remote and other developers are building on it.
questions.explanation: Rebasing rewrites commit SHAs. If others have based work on the original SHAs, rewriting them creates a divergent history that is very painful to reconcile. Only rebase branches you own exclusively and haven't shared with others.

questions.prompt: A commit message says: 'feat(checkout): add promo code validation and fix null pointer in payment service and update checkout README'. What is wrong?
options: The scope is wrong — it should be empty
The commit contains multiple unrelated changes — should be split into at least 2 commits
Nothing — this is a thorough commit message
questions.answer: The commit contains multiple unrelated changes — should be split into at least 2 commits
questions.explanation: A commit should be atomic — one logical change. This message describes three separate changes: a feature (promo validation), a bug fix (NPE), and documentation. Split into: feat(checkout): add promo code validation, fix(payment): prevent NPE in payment service, docs(checkout): update checkout README.
